The larval period of Queensland dwarfgoby (Eviota queenslandica) is remarkably brief, with yolk-sac larvae hatching after approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days] at a water temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. These prolarvae emerge at a wet weight of just 0.00012 grams [Wwb = 0.00012 grams], a minute initial mass that is consistent with the very small egg diameters observed in congeneric species. The rapid pace of early development is a hallmark of this diminutive taxon and sets the stage for an extremely compressed life cycle.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a standard length of only 1.31 centimeters [Lp = 1.31 centimeters], at which point individuals have typically attained a wet weight of approximately 0.009 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.009 grams]. This size at the onset of gonadal activity is considerably smaller than the maximum ultimate standard length of 2.4 centimeters [Li = 2.4 centimeters] that the fish eventually achieve. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of 0.21 grams [Wwi = 0.21 grams] represents a more than twentyfold increase in mass from the pubertal stage, indicating that a substantial portion of somatic growth occurs after reproductive maturity has already been reached.

Reproductive investment in this goby is compressed into a very short adult phase under the warm thermal regime of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. Lab-reared females at this temperature exhibit a lifetime fecundity of 1039 eggs per day , an exceptionally high output for a fish of this body size at a temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. This prodigious fecundity is made possible by an iteroparous spawning strategy in which females produce clutches repeatedly over their brief adult lifespan, and it reflects the selective pressure to maximize offspring number before senescence intervenes.

The maximum longevity documented for Queensland dwarfgoby is 99.0 days [am = 99.0 days] at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], a lifespan that places it among the shortest-lived of all known vertebrates. This abbreviated existence, from the moment of hatching to natural death, constrains the species to a single, intense reproductive window. The brief duration of the post-settlement juvenile stage means that individuals must transition from first exogenous feeding to a spawning adult within a matter of weeks, a rapid pace that is mirrored in other small-bodied coral-reef gobies.

Ecologically, this compressed life history is tightly linked to the predictable, warm conditions of its shallow reef habitat. The larval and adult stages alike are optimized for the stable thermal environment near 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], where metabolic rates are elevated and development proceeds at its fastest possible pace. Comparisons with larger-bodied gobiids that inhabit cooler waters reveal that the dwarfgoby's extreme pace of life — which begins at a hatchling mass of just 0.00012 grams [Wwb = 0.00012 grams], an order of magnitude smaller than that of related reef fishes — represents an adaptive response to high predation pressure and ephemeral habitat patches typical of tropical coral rubble zones.
